cards.explanation: The answer is three months, friends. The text says, “After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island.” (Acts 28:11) That's a long stretch on one island. The ship they boarded had spent the winter there too.

The brothers invite the group to stay with them. The text says they found brothers “…who invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Fellow believers, and they invite the group to stay. A good host is a gift, friends.
The answer is week. The text says the brothers “…invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Seven days of company before the road to Rome. I'd take that kind of invitation any day.

The answer is True. “When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.” (Acts 28:15) The believers had heard about the group and traveled out to meet them. Paul saw friendly faces on the road, and he thanked God right there. I think seeing them did him a world of good.

Paul gets to stay by himself with a soldier to guard him, bakers. The text says Paul “…was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.” (Acts 28:16) He's still a prisoner, since a soldier guards him. But he gets to stay by himself. I think that's a lot better than what I'd have expected for a prisoner.

The answer is True. Paul tells them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.” (Acts 28:17) He opens by calling them brothers and telling them where he stands. Then he tells them how he ended up in chains.

The Romans wanted to let him go free, friends. Paul says they “…examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) They looked into it and wanted him released. I've had cookies inspected before, and I never got a verdict that clean.

The answer is False. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, “…even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.” (Acts 28:19) He has no charge to bring against his nation. What he says is that when the Jews objected, he was compelled to appeal.

His reason is the hope of Israel, friends, and he doesn't dodge it. “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20) No crime on his list, just the hope of Israel. I bet he'd say that one out loud all day.

The leaders want to hear his views. They say it plainly: “…we consider your views worth hearing…” (Acts 28:22). They tell Paul they've received no letters about him from Judea, and none of the brothers from there reported or mentioned anything bad about him (Acts 28:21). So they're willing to listen to him themselves. Not a bad way to open a conversation.

The answer is False. The leaders say, “…we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.” (Acts 28:22) They've heard people speaking against it, not welcoming it. Even so, they say Paul's views are worth hearing.

Paul teaches from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, friends. He was “…persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.” (Acts 28:23) He used Scripture, and he taught from morning to evening. It's a long day, and I think he knew his material.

Some are convinced and others refuse. “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.” (Acts 28:24) It was a split, and they disagreed among themselves. Same message, same day, different answers.

The reason in Isaiah's words is that their heart has grown callous. “For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.” (Acts 28:27) A callous heart is a hardened one. The words say they have closed their eyes, too.

The answer is True. Paul says the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah the prophet (Acts 28:25), and those words say, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Acts 28:27) Seeing, hearing, understanding and turning come first. Then comes the healing.

The answer is the Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish. Paul says, “Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (Acts 28:28) That's a big announcement, and he says they will listen.

Paul welcomes all who come to visit him, friends. He stayed “…in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him.” (Acts 28:30) All who came, with no list of who could knock. That's a welcome I'd be proud of.

The answer is False. The text says, “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.” (Acts 28:31) He didn't hold back, even as a prisoner. Boldly and freely, that's how the story ends.
